**Endosymbiosis and reductive evolution** — how one organism comes to live inside another and depend on it, and how that ends — reductive genome evolution by drift, deletional bias or adaptive loss (including the Black Queen dependencies of free-living microbes), complementary loss across partners, nested symbioses and symbiont splitting and replacement, endosymbiotic gene transfer, protein import and host control of transmission, organellogenesis and organelle loss, and eukaryogenesis. The ecology of a partnership is ecology (ADR-055).

| [QUESTION-277](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-277.md) v5 | When formerly autonomous partners come to depend on one another, which of mutual dependence, reproductive cohesion, the distribution of essential functions across genomes, the host's regulatory control and the alignment of selection does each route to dependence bring about, and which of them, alone or together, make the partnership a new evolutionary individual? | From the exchange of 2026-10-27 on the record's coverage of reductive evolution and endosymbiosis. Dependence can come from selection for individual gene loss ([LIT-1568](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1568.md)), from drift in small symbiont populations ([LIT-1573](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1573.md)), from complementary loss across lineages ([LIT-1565](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1565.md), [LIT-1563](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1563.md)) or from gene transfer and protein import ([LIT-1557](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1557.md), [LIT-1562](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1562.md)). None of these is selection for the collective. Athreya et al. ([LIT-1570](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1570.md)) model dependence and cohesion as separate properties that evolve at different rates. An answer would say, route by route and on real systems, which properties each produces, and which of them a theory of individuality must require. All the works cited are filed unread. | Open |
